guidance: Preliminary engineering estimate—verify loads, materials, governing standards, and calculations with a qualified engineer before fabrication or construction.
method: The page treats the screw as a block sliding on the unwrapped thread: one turn flattens into a right triangle with a base of the circumference at the mean thread diameter, pi dm, and a height equal to the lead, so the lead angle is lambda = arctan(l / (pi dm)) with l = starts x pitch. Resolving the axial load F along that incline against a friction angle phi = arctan(mu) gives the torque to raise the load T = (F dm / 2) tan(phi + lambda) and the torque to lower it (F dm / 2) tan(phi - lambda). A thread flank that is not square also carries the load wedged on its inclined faces, so every mu becomes mu sec(alpha) with alpha the half thread angle - 30 degrees for an ISO metric or unified 60 degree thread, 14.5 degrees for a 29 degree Acme, 0 for square or buttress - which is the published form (F dm / 2)(l + pi mu dm sec(alpha)) / (pi dm - mu l sec(alpha)). The mean diameter is the pitch diameter: dm = d - 0.649519 P for a 60 degree thread, from the 0.375 H offset of the basic ISO profile, and dm = d - 0.5 P for Acme, trapezoidal and square threads, whose thread height is half the pitch. A collar that carries the load adds Tc = F mu_c d_c / 2 at its mean radius, with mu_c and d_c entered separately and d_c = 0 for a thrust bearing, so the raising torque reported first is the thread plus the collar. The efficiency is the work delivered over the work put in, eta = F l / (2 pi T), reported once with the collar and once for the thread alone, and it is also tabulated as tan(lambda) / tan(phi + lambda) for the bare thread. The lowering torque is reported as a magnitude in the lowering direction: it is positive when friction holds the load (mu sec(alpha) >= tan(lambda), the self-locking condition, so the page prints zero and says the screw holds the load without a brake) and negative when the lead is steep enough that the load drives the screw down and a brake or a holding motor is needed. Whether the collar alone is enough to stop that run-down is reported separately. A worked default: an M30 x 3.5 single start raising 10 kN with mu = 0.15, a 40 mm collar at mu_c = 0.10 gives a mean diameter of 27.727 mm, a lead angle of 2.30 degrees, 29.79 N m in the thread, 20.00 N m in the collar, 49.79 N m total and 11.19 percent overall efficiency, and it self-locks because the 9.83 degree friction angle exceeds the lead angle. Inputs are bounded: load 0.001 to 5000 kN, nominal diameter 1 to 600 mm, pitch 0.2 to 50 mm and always under half the diameter, starts 1 to 8 whole numbers, both friction coefficients 0 to 0.5, and mean collar diameter 0 to 2000 mm. A lead so steep against the thread friction that pi dm - mu l sec(alpha) would reach zero is refused rather than returned as an unbounded torque. This is a steady uniform-load friction model of one thread: it does not check thread or nut bearing and shear stress, buckling of a long screw, wear, running-in, the critical speed, starting torque or the vibration and shock that can drop the effective friction and let a nominally self-locking screw back-drive, so it sizes a drive rather than qualifying one. Everything runs locally in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
